title: Cork Oak: Ancient Cork Oaks You Can Visit
meta_description: A working cork oak is stripped bare every nine years. Portugal's Whistler gave 1,200 kilos of cork in one stripping and was Europe's tree of the year.
intro: A working cork oak gets stripped to the bare wood every nine years or so, its bark peeled off in slabs for wine corks and flooring. The Whistler at Aguas de Moura in Portugal has been harvested more than twenty times since around 1820; a single stripping in 1991 gave more than 1,200 kilos, and in 2018 it won European Tree of the Year. The ones in gardens were never harvested, so they carry what the industry takes away: an outer bark up to thirty centimetres thick, spongy enough that pressing a thumb into it is half the reason to go. Sintra's is the Sobreira dos Fetos, the Fern Cork Oak, because ferns grow straight out of its bark; Portugal's register puts it at 350 years. The oak in Rome's orangery was measured twice in three years and grew from 5.00 metres around to 5.30 in between.
